text: Range looks simple, but it has three forms that unlock a lot of control.
With one argument, it counts from zero up to, but not including, that number.
[chuckle] Give it two arguments and you set both the start and the stop yourself.
So two to eight gives you two, three, four, five, six, and seven — stopping just before eight.
[sniff] A third argument is the step, the size of each jump — here we count up by fives.
And a negative step counts backwards, letting you walk from ten down to zero by twos.
[sigh] Here's the beautiful part — range is lazy, it never actually stores all those numbers.
A range of a million takes almost no memory, yet you can still index it or ask its length instantly.
[groan] So range isn't a list, it's a smart recipe for numbers, generated only as you need them.
